pumac-2014-finals-a-01.title: The circle BCI has centre L with LI = AI/2
pumac-2014-finals-a-01.body:
Let $a=BC$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$, $s=\frac{a+b+c}2$, $\alpha=\angle A$, $r$ the inradius. From $b+c=3a$ we get $s=2a$ and $AD=s-a=a$.

*Lengths along $AI$.* In the right triangle $ADI$ (right angle at $D$), $AI\cos\frac\alpha2=AD=a$, so $AI=\dfrac a{\cos(\alpha/2)}$. Let $L$ be the midpoint of arc $BC$ of the circumcircle (not containing $A$). By the incenter–excenter lemma, $L$ lies on ray $AI$ beyond $I$, $LB=LC=LI$, so $L$ is the centre of circle $BCI$. In the isosceles triangle $BLC$ the apex angle is $180^\circ-\alpha$, hence $LI=LB=\dfrac{a/2}{\cos(\alpha/2)}=\dfrac{AI}2$.

*The antipode $D'$ of $D$ lies on circle $BCI$.* Take $I$ as origin, $e$ the unit vector from $A$ towards $I$, so $A=-AI\,e$ and $L=\frac{AI}2e$. Let $d=\vec{ID}$, $|d|=r$. Since $ID\perp AD$, $d\cdot(d-A)=0$, so $r^2=d\cdot A=-AI\,(d\cdot e)$, i.e. $d\cdot e=-\dfrac{r^2}{AI}$. The antipode is $D'=-d$ and
$$|D'-L|^2=\left|d+\tfrac{AI}2e\right|^2=r^2+\tfrac{AI^2}4+AI\,(d\cdot e)=\tfrac{AI^2}4=LI^2 .$$
So $D'$ lies on circle $BCI$ (centre $L$, radius $LI$) and on $\gamma$.

*$D'$ is the intersection closer to $B$.* Both circles are symmetric about line $AI$, so their two common points are $D'$ and its mirror image $E'$ (the antipode of the tangency point on $AB$). $D$ lies on $AC$, which is on the $C$-side of line $AI$; the point reflection in $I$ sends it to the other side, so $D'$ is on the $B$-side of $AI$. Of two points symmetric about a line, the one on the same side as $B$ is closer to $B$, hence $P=D'$.

Since $D'$ is the reflection of $D$ in $I$, the points $P,I,D$ are collinear. ∎

pumac-2014-finals-a-02.title: Tangent line trick through AM-GM
pumac-2014-finals-a-02.body:
For each variable,
$$\frac1{a^3+2}=\frac12\left(1-\frac{a^3}{a^3+2}\right).$$
By AM–GM, $a^3+1+1\ge3a$, i.e. $a^3+2\ge3a>0$, so $\dfrac{a^3}{a^3+2}\le\dfrac{a^3}{3a}=\dfrac{a^2}3$. Hence
$$\frac1{a^3+2}\ge\frac12\left(1-\frac{a^2}3\right)=\frac12-\frac{a^2}6,$$
and the same for $b$ and $c$. Adding,
$$\sum\frac1{a^3+2}\ge\frac32-\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}6=\frac32-\frac12=1.$$
Equality holds at $a=b=c=1$. ∎

pumac-2014-finals-a-03.title: Linear algebra over the field with two elements
pumac-2014-finals-a-03.body:
Encode $+$ as $0$ and $-$ as $1$, so a position is a vector $a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb F_2^n$ (indices mod $n$). Coin $k$ is flipped iff its neighbours differ, i.e. $a_{k-1}+a_{k+1}=1$. So the new value is $a_k+a_{k-1}+a_{k+1}$ (mod $2$): a flop is the linear map $T=I+S+S^{-1}$, where $S$ is the cyclic shift.

**(b)** *If $3\mid n$,* take the arrangement $++-\,++-\cdots++-$. In the pattern $(+,+,-)$ each $+$ coin has one $+$ and one $-$ neighbour and is flipped, while the $-$ coin has two $+$ neighbours and stays; so one flop gives all $-$, and an all-equal arrangement never changes. So it never returns to the start: no perfect number.

*If $3\nmid n$,* $T$ is injective: if $Ta=0$ then $a_{k-1}+a_k+a_{k+1}=0$ for all $k$, hence $a_{k+2}=a_{k-1}$ (compare consecutive equations), so $a$ has period $3$; it also has period $n$ and $\gcd(3,n)=1$, so $a$ is constant, say $a_k=c$, and $3c=c=0$. So $T$ is a bijection of the finite set $\mathbb F_2^n$, and its order $M$ (a finite number) satisfies $T^M=I$: $M$ is a perfect number.

So a perfect number exists iff $3\nmid n$.

**(a)** In characteristic $2$, squaring is additive, so $T^{2^j}=I+S^{2^j}+S^{-2^j}$. For $n=1024$ and $j=9$: $S^{512}=S^{-512}$ since $S^{1024}=I$, so
$$T^{512}=I+2S^{512}=I.$$
Hence $M=512$ is a perfect number (and any multiple of $512$ is one as well; $M=256$ fails since $T^{256}=I+S^{256}+S^{-256}\ne I$). ∎
